messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sami, a 48-year-old Middle Eastern man and a fashion designer, has been struggling to cope with the aftermath of a man-made disaster that he experienced several months ago. The event was so traumatic that it left him with fragmented memories that often feel like they are happening all over again. Sami’s daily life is punctuated by sudden intrusive memories that bring back vivid sensory details from the trauma. One such trigger occurred recently while he was at work, feeling a specific temperature on his skin that matched the ambient temperature of the disaster scene. The memory hit him so forcefully that he felt nauseous and had to excuse himself from the bustling design studio where he works. This is when Sami’s maladaptive strategies kicked in; he would often hurt himself physically to release the overwhelming feelings, or work himself into a frenzy by keeping busy with other tasks. The fragmented nature of his memories has made it difficult for him to piece together what happened during the disaster. The memory feels present and not past, and when triggered, it is accompanied by a vivid taste that he associates with the event. This disjointed recollection often leads to an acute sense of danger, which drives Sami’s heightened threat monitoring behaviors. He constantly scans his surroundings for signs of danger and always identifies escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere. These fragmented memories also lead directly to his maladaptive strategies. When a memory intrudes, he becomes hyper-focused on the details, unable to concentrate on anything else. To cope with this intense focus, Sami resorts to self-harm or busyness to distract himself from the overwhelming sense of danger and discomfort. The trauma has significantly impacted his work environment. His need for constant distraction through busyness means that he often neglects important tasks, leading to increased stress and tension in his professional relationships. Additionally, the repeated checking of locks and windows at home is a clear sign that Sami’s maladaptive strategies are deeply intertwined with his threat perception. Sami’s fear has grown into a self-reinforcing cycle over time. The more he focuses on the fragmented memories and their vivid sensory details, the greater his sense of danger becomes. This heightened state then leads him to engage in even more maladaptive behaviors as coping mechanisms, further exacerbating his condition. He has come to believe that he needs to be constantly vigilant and prepared for any potential threat. What finally brought Sami to seek help was a combination of mounting stress at work and the realization that his self-harm had escalated to a point where it could no longer be ignored. He is most afraid of losing control over these intense feelings, but he also hopes for a way to regain some sense of normalcy in his daily life. Sami’s story illustrates how the traumatic event has led him into a cycle of intrusive memories, heightened threat perceptions, and maladaptive coping strategies that have significantly impacted both his personal and professional life.
